segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. He went to see them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue and tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself wholly to the word, solemnly testifying to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they opposed him and became abusive, he shook out his clothes and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Your blood be on your own head! I am clean of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he moved from there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Crispus, the synagogue leader, believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid, but keep speaking and do not be silent,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he settled there for a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up together against Paul and brought him before the tribunal,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If this were a matter of some wrongdoing or vicious crime, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to bear with you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But if these are disputes about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I have no wish to be a judge of these things.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he drove them away from the tribunal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and began beating him in front of the tribunal. But none of this was of any concern to Gallio.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul stayed on for a good many days, then took leave of the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. At Cenchreae he had his hair cut off, for he was under a vow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They arrived in Ephesus, and there he left them. He himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they asked him to stay longer, he did not consent,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but took his leave and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I will come back to you again, if God wills.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He set sail from Ephesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the assembly, and then went down to Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After spending some time there he set out and went from place to place through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, arrived in Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the Scriptures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he wanted to cross over to Achaia, the brothers and sisters encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. On his arrival he was a great help to those who had believed through grace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing through the Scriptures that the Messiah was Jesus.

notes.phrase: Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome
notes.note: The emperor Claudius (reigned AD 41–54) expelled Jews from Rome, an event the Roman biographer Suetonius also mentions. It is commonly dated to about AD 49, though the date is not certain. How thoroughly the order was enforced is also unknown; “all” may be a general statement.

The word is rare. It literally names a maker of tents, but many scholars think it covered leatherworking more broadly, since tents were often made of leather. The traditional rendering is kept because the narrower sense cannot be ruled out.

The Greek word is the one usually rendered “Christ”. Here it is a title under debate in a synagogue, the anointed king Israel expected, so “Messiah” is used, as several modern translations do. The Greek can also be read “that Jesus was the Messiah”; the sense is much the same.

Shaking out one's garments was a gesture of breaking off and disowning responsibility (compare Nehemiah 5:13). The words that follow echo the language of Ezekiel 33, where a watchman who has given warning is free of blame for the death of those who ignore it.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and this translation then renders it “Gentiles”; elsewhere the same word appears as “nation” or “nations”.

In Acts this phrase describes Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue and honoured Israel's God without becoming full converts. Titius Justus bears a Roman name and was evidently such a person.

Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca. An inscription found at Delphi places his term as governor of the province of Achaia in about AD 51–52, which makes this one of the firmest dates in the chronology of Paul's life. The tribunal was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases.

The accusers do not say whether they mean Roman law or the Jewish law. They may have intended the charge to sound like a breach of Roman law; Gallio takes it as a dispute about “your own law” and dismisses it.

The earliest manuscripts do not say who “all” are. Many later manuscripts add “the Greeks”, the reading behind the King James Version, making this a bystanders' attack on the Jewish leader; a few add “the Jews”. Either group is possible, and the text is left as open as the Greek.

notes.phrase: he had his hair cut off
notes.note: Cenchreae was Corinth's eastern port, so the haircut preceded the sailing. In the Greek the one who cut his hair could be either Paul or Aquila, whose name stands immediately before; most interpreters take it to be Paul, the subject of the sentence. Cutting the hair normally marked the completion of a vow such as the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, though Luke gives no details.

The traditional rendering is “church”, which readers know but which now suggests a building or an institution. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The Greek does not name the place. “Go up” and “go down” are the usual expressions for travelling to and from Jerusalem, so most interpreters understand a visit to the assembly in Jerusalem. A minority take it to mean going up from the harbour to the assembly in Caesarea.

The Greek is literally “boiling in the spirit”. It can describe Apollos's own ardent temperament, as rendered here, or mean that he was aglow with the Holy Spirit. The second reading is disputed because Apollos is said to have known only John's baptism.

The phrase stands at the end of the Greek sentence and can attach to either verb. The believers came to believe through grace, or Apollos through grace was a great help to them. The rendering follows the nearer connection.

candidates.reason: The plural for members of the believing community recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; it needs one policy.
The word covers both abuse aimed at people and blasphemy against God, and the choice between “revile/slander” and “blaspheme” recurs across the Gospels, Acts and the letters.
It is rendered variously as “tribunal”, “judgment seat” or “judge's bench”, and it recurs in the trial narratives and in Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, where consistency shows the shared image.
The participle for Gentile synagogue adherents recurs in Acts 13–18 and is rendered variously as “God-fearer”, “devout” or “worshipper of God”; it should be fixed alongside φοβούμενος τὸν θεόν.
It is Luke's regular word for Paul's activity in synagogues (Acts 17–20, 24), and translators vary between “reasoned”, “argued”, “debated” and “held discussions”.
